fha.title: FHA Loans
fha.description: Flexible requirements for FHA loans in Florida.
fha.heading: FHA Loans
fha.heroTitle: A smaller down payment doesn't have to stop you
fha.heroSub: If your savings are limited or your credit history isn't perfect, an FHA loan keeps the door open.
fha.blurb: Flexible credit requirements and a down payment as low as 3.5%. Often the first step into homeownership.
fha.intro: An FHA loan is insured by the federal government, which is why lenders can approve buyers that conventional programs sometimes turn away. It's built for people who are still building credit or savings, not for those who already have both figured out. I use it often with first-time buyers.

whatIs.title: What is an FHA loan?
whatIs.body: An FHA loan is a mortgage insured by the Federal Housing Administration, a federal agency, so the lender takes on less risk than with a conventional loan. That backing is what lets you qualify with a down payment from 3.5% and a credit score that a conventional program might not accept. In exchange, you'll pay mortgage insurance for part or all of the loan term, unlike a conventional loan where it can usually be removed once you build enough equity.

required.title: What do you need for an FHA loan?
required.body: You'll need proof of income, two years of work history, and a credit score that meets the program minimum — flexible, but not without requirements. The home has to be your primary residence, not a rental or vacation property. A past bankruptcy or foreclosure doesn't automatically disqualify you, but there's a waiting period I'll confirm with you case by case. I'll tell you which documents to gather before you start looking at homes.

how.title: How an FHA loan works
items: Down payments starting at 3.5% of the purchase price.
Fixed terms commonly available in 15 or 30 years.
Mortgage insurance included in your monthly payment, for part or all of the loan.
No penalty for paying off the loan early.

conventional.title: Conventional Loans
conventional.heading: Conventional Loans
conventional.heroTitle: Solid credit opens the door to better terms
conventional.heroSub: If your credit and income are already strong, a conventional loan usually costs you less over time.
conventional.blurb: Competitive rates and terms if your credit is solid. Down payments starting around 3%.
conventional.intro: A conventional loan is the standard mortgage — not backed by a government agency, and usually the better deal once your credit and savings are established. It rewards a stronger financial profile with lower long-term costs. I compare it against FHA for almost every buyer who qualifies for both.

whatIs.title: What is a conventional loan?
whatIs.body: A conventional loan is a mortgage that isn't insured or guaranteed by a government agency, which means the lender relies more heavily on your credit and income. With solid credit, it typically comes with a down payment starting around 3%, competitive rates, and terms that can be more flexible than FHA. Unlike FHA, the mortgage insurance on a conventional loan can usually be removed once you reach a set level of equity — often around 20%.

required.title: What do you need for a conventional loan?
required.body: Lenders generally look for a stronger credit score than FHA requires, along with steady income and two years of employment history. Down payments start around 3%, though a larger down payment can lower your rate and remove mortgage insurance sooner. You can use it for a primary residence, a second home, or an investment property, which FHA doesn't allow. I'll walk through your credit report with you before we apply, so there are no surprises.

how.title: How a conventional loan works
items: Down payments starting around 3%, higher for second homes or investment properties.
Fixed terms commonly available in 15, 20, or 30 years.
Mortgage insurance that can be removed once you build enough equity.
No penalty for paying off the loan early.

va.title: VA Loans
va.description: VA loan benefits for veterans and service members.
va.heading: VA Loans
va.heroTitle: Buy with $0 down, backed by your service
va.heroSub: If you served, your benefit can cover the down payment most other buyers have to save for.
va.blurb: A benefit earned through service — often no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance.
va.intro: A VA loan is a benefit for eligible veterans, active-duty service members, and some surviving spouses, guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs. It's one of the few programs that can finance a home with no down payment at all. I confirm your eligibility first, before we talk about anything else.

whatIs.title: What is a VA loan?
whatIs.body: A VA loan is a mortgage guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs for eligible veterans, active-duty service members, and certain surviving spouses. The guarantee is what allows lenders to offer it with no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, which sets it apart from both FHA and conventional loans. You'll pay a one-time funding fee in most cases, though some borrowers are exempt.

required.title: What do you need for a VA loan?
required.body: You'll need a Certificate of Eligibility, which confirms your service meets the program's requirements — I can help you request it if you don't already have one. There's no minimum down payment and no fixed minimum credit score from the VA itself, though lenders apply their own guidelines. The home must be your primary residence. Credit flexibility is real, but your income and debt still have to support the payment.

how.title: How a VA loan works
items: No down payment required in most cases.
No monthly mortgage insurance.
Fixed terms commonly available in 15 or 30 years.
A one-time funding fee, waived for some borrowers with a service-connected disability.

firstTimeHomebuyer.title: First Time Homebuyer
firstTimeHomebuyer.description: Programs for first time homebuyers in Florida.
firstTimeHomebuyer.heading: First Time Homebuyer
firstTimeHomebuyer.heroTitle: Florida help for your first down payment
firstTimeHomebuyer.heroSub: If saving for a down payment feels like the hardest part, Florida assistance programs may cover more of it than you think.
firstTimeHomebuyer.blurb: Down payment and closing cost assistance for first-time buyers in Florida, paired with FHA or conventional financing.
firstTimeHomebuyer.intro: First-time buyer programs aren't a separate loan — they're assistance layered on top of an FHA or conventional mortgage to help with the down payment and closing costs. Florida offers several of these, and most buyers never ask about them. I check what you qualify for before you start house hunting, not after.

whatIs.title: What is first-time homebuyer assistance?
whatIs.body: First-time homebuyer assistance combines a standard mortgage — usually FHA or conventional — with a Florida program that helps cover your down payment or closing costs, sometimes as a grant and sometimes as a low-interest second loan. It's not a different type of mortgage; it's help layered on top of one you'd already qualify for. The programs available and how much they cover change depending on income, location, and purchase price.

required.title: What do you need for first-time buyer assistance?
required.body: You'll generally need to be purchasing your first home — or your first home in several years, depending on the program — and your household income has to fall within the program's limits. You'll still go through the same credit and income approval as any FHA or conventional loan. Some programs require a short homebuyer education course, which I'll point you to if it applies. I'll tell you upfront which programs you're likely to qualify for.

how.title: How first-time buyer assistance works
items: Paired with an FHA or conventional loan, not a standalone mortgage.
Covers part of your down payment or closing costs, as a grant or a second loan.
Income limits that vary by county and household size.
Some programs require a short homebuyer education course.

refinance.title: Refinance
refinance.heading: Refinance
refinance.heroTitle: Lower your payment, or put your equity to work
refinance.heroSub: If your rate, your term, or your monthly payment no longer fits, refinancing might be worth a look.
refinance.blurb: Lower your rate, shorten your term, remove mortgage insurance, or take cash out from your equity.
refinance.intro: Refinancing replaces your current mortgage with a new one, on new terms. Sometimes it's about a lower monthly payment, sometimes about paying off the home faster, and sometimes about pulling out equity you've already built. It only makes sense in some cases — I'll tell you honestly when it doesn't.

whatIs.title: What is a refinance?
whatIs.body: Refinancing means paying off your current mortgage with a new loan, ideally on better terms. That can mean a lower interest rate, a shorter or longer term, the removal of mortgage insurance once you have enough equity, or a cash-out refinance that lets you borrow against the value you've built. The right move depends on your current rate, how long you plan to stay, and what you're trying to solve.

required.title: What do you need to refinance?
required.body: You'll need enough equity in your home — the exact amount depends on the type of refinance — along with income and credit that support the new loan. A cash-out refinance usually requires more equity than a rate-and-term refinance. Closing costs apply, similar to a purchase, so I run the numbers to see how long it takes to break even. If the math doesn't work in your favor, I'll say so.

how.title: How a refinance works
items: Replaces your current mortgage with a new rate, term, or loan amount.
Cash-out option lets you borrow against your home's equity.
Closing costs apply, similar to a home purchase.
A break-even point tells you how long it takes to come out ahead.

fixedRate.title: Fixed Rate Mortgage
fixedRate.description: One rate and one payment for the life of your loan.
fixedRate.heading: Fixed Rate Mortgage
fixedRate.heroTitle: One payment that never surprises you
fixedRate.heroSub: Lock your rate once and your principal-and-interest payment stays the same until the loan is paid off.
fixedRate.blurb: The most predictable way to borrow: rate and payment locked from day one, whether you choose 15, 20, or 30 years.
fixedRate.intro: A fixed rate mortgage is less a program than a promise: the rate you close with is the rate you keep. Most of the loans I write — FHA, conventional, VA — can be structured this way. If you plan to stay in your home and want a housing cost you can build a budget around, this is the default I start from.

whatIs.title: What is a fixed rate mortgage?
whatIs.body: It's a loan where the interest rate is set at closing and never changes, so the principal-and-interest portion of your payment is identical in month one and in the final month. The alternative — an adjustable rate — starts lower but can move with the market after the initial period. Fixed means you trade a slightly higher starting rate for certainty that no rate hike can touch your payment.

required.title: What do you need for a fixed rate mortgage?
required.body: The same fundamentals as the underlying program you qualify for: verifiable income, a manageable debt load, and a credit profile that fits the loan type — flexible with FHA, stricter with conventional. There's no extra requirement for choosing fixed over adjustable. What matters is picking the term: a shorter term costs more per month and far less in total interest, and I'll show you both numbers before you decide.

how.title: How a fixed rate mortgage works
items: Your rate is locked at closing and never changes with the market.
Terms commonly available in 30, 20, or 15 years — shorter term, less total interest.
Early payments are mostly interest; over time more of each payment builds equity.
No penalty for paying it off early with the programs I work with.

usda.title: USDA Loans
usda.description: USDA loan options for eligible rural and suburban areas in Florida.
usda.heading: USDA Loans
usda.heroTitle: Own a home with no down payment at all
usda.heroSub: In USDA-eligible areas outside the urban core, you can finance 100% of the purchase.
usda.blurb: Backed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture: 0% down in eligible rural and suburban areas.
usda.intro: A USDA loan is backed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which is why it can finance a home with zero down payment. It's built for buyers purchasing in eligible rural and suburban areas — not a program for every location. Most people assume it doesn't apply to them; in Florida, the eligible map is wider than you'd guess. I check the address first, before anything else.

whatIs.title: What is a USDA loan?
whatIs.body: A USDA loan is a mortgage guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, designed to expand homeownership outside major urban centers. That guarantee lets you finance up to 100% of the purchase price, with no down payment required. Eligibility works on two tracks at once: the property has to sit inside a USDA-designated area, and your household income has to fall under the program's limit for that area. In place of traditional mortgage insurance, you'll pay a guarantee fee, which is generally lower over time. It's a primary-residence program only — no investment properties or vacation homes.

required.title: What do you need for a USDA loan?
required.body: The property is the first thing I check — it has to fall inside a USDA-eligible area, which in Florida covers more towns and outskirts than most buyers expect. From there, your household income needs to stay under the program's limit, which varies by area and family size. You'll still need steady income, an acceptable credit profile, and the home has to be your primary residence. I run the address and your numbers together before we go any further, so we don't waste time chasing a home that won't qualify.

how.title: How a USDA loan works
items: No down payment required for an eligible property in an eligible area.
Eligibility depends on both the property's location and your household income.
A guarantee fee replaces traditional mortgage insurance, often at a lower ongoing cost.
Limited to primary residences — not available for investment or vacation properties.

jumbo.title: Jumbo Loans
jumbo.description: Jumbo loan financing above the conforming limit in Florida.
jumbo.heading: Jumbo Loans
jumbo.heroSub: For homes priced above the conforming loan limit, a jumbo loan takes over where standard programs stop.
jumbo.blurb: For amounts above the conforming limit — common in Miami's market — with competitive rates for strong profiles.
jumbo.intro: A jumbo loan is for homes priced above the conforming loan limit — the ceiling that Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac set for standard mortgages. That limit changes every year and by county, and I confirm the current number before we talk about your specific home. It's not a niche product in Miami: at today's prices, plenty of buyers need one without realizing it.

whatIs.title: What is a jumbo loan?
whatIs.body: A jumbo loan finances an amount above the conforming loan limit, which means it falls outside the guidelines Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac use to back standard mortgages. Because the lender can't sell the loan to those agencies, it holds more of the risk directly, and underwriting reflects that. You'll generally see a stronger credit score requirement, proof of cash reserves after closing, and a larger down payment than a conforming loan asks for. In a market like Miami, where home prices routinely land above the conforming ceiling, a jumbo loan is often the only path to the property you want.

required.title: What do you need for a jumbo loan?
required.body: Expect a higher bar across the board: a stronger credit score, a lower debt-to-income ratio, and documented reserves — savings left over after closing — that a conforming loan wouldn't ask for. The down payment typically runs higher than the low-down-payment programs allow, though the exact number depends on the loan amount and your profile. I'll pull the current conforming limit for your county before we start, since it changes and determines whether your loan is even considered jumbo. Income and asset documentation tend to be more thorough, and I walk you through exactly what to gather.

how.title: How a jumbo loan works
items: Finances amounts above the conforming loan limit, which is set annually by county.
Requires a stronger credit score and documented cash reserves after closing.
Down payments typically higher than standard conforming programs.
Common in Miami, where home prices often exceed the conforming ceiling.

lowDownPayment.title: Low Down Payment Options
lowDownPayment.description: Compare every low down payment path: FHA, conventional, VA, and USDA.
lowDownPayment.heading: Low Down Payment Options
lowDownPayment.heroTitle: The down payment is smaller than you think
lowDownPayment.heroSub: Between FHA, conventional 3% programs, VA and USDA, saving 20% is optional — not a requirement.
lowDownPayment.blurb: A map of every path to buying with little money upfront: which program fits depends on your profile, and comparing them is my job.
lowDownPayment.intro: Twenty percent down is a myth that keeps good buyers renting longer than they need to. Between FHA at 3.5%, conventional programs starting around 3%, and VA or USDA at zero, most buyers qualify for something well below that number. Which one fits you depends on your credit, your income, and the kind of property you're after — comparing them honestly is where I start every conversation.

whatIs.title: What counts as a low down payment?
whatIs.body: Low down payment covers every path that gets you into a home without the traditional 20%: FHA at 3.5%, conventional loans starting around 3%, and VA or USDA loans that can finance 100% for qualified buyers. Each comes with trade-offs — a smaller down payment usually means mortgage insurance until you build equity, and in a competitive market a low-down offer can be harder for a seller to choose over one with more cash. Down payment assistance programs, grants and low-interest second loans, can also cover part of what's left. None of this is one-size-fits-all, which is why I compare your options side by side instead of defaulting to one.

required.title: What do you need for a low down payment purchase?
required.body: What you need depends entirely on which path fits: FHA asks for more flexible credit, conventional rewards a stronger score with a lower rate, and VA or USDA can eliminate the down payment altogether if you qualify. In every case, lenders still want steady income and manageable debt — a low down payment doesn't mean low scrutiny elsewhere. If a 20% down payment isn't realistic right now, tell me that upfront; it changes which programs I run the numbers on first, and whether assistance programs make sense for your situation. The quote questionnaire is usually the fastest way to see where you land.

how.title: How low down payment options compare
items: FHA starts at 3.5% down; conventional programs can start around 3%.
VA and USDA can finance up to 100%, for buyers who qualify.
A smaller down payment usually means paying mortgage insurance until you build equity.
Down payment assistance programs can cover part of what's left, evaluated case by case.

investment.title: Investment Property Loans
investment.description: Financing options for investment and rental properties in Florida.
investment.heading: Investment Property Loans
investment.heroTitle: Make the property pay for itself
investment.heroSub: Financing built for rentals: programs where the property's income matters as much as yours.
investment.blurb: For buying rental property: conventional investor loans and programs that qualify by the property's rental income.
investment.intro: Financing a rental property works differently than financing the home you live in. Lenders typically ask for a larger down payment and charge a somewhat higher rate, because an investment property carries more risk than a primary residence. Some programs go a step further and qualify you using the property's own rental income rather than your personal one. Whether this is your first rental or the next addition to a growing portfolio, I run both paths before we pick one.

whatIs.title: What is an investment property loan?
whatIs.body: An investment property loan finances a home you don't plan to live in — a single rental, a small multi-unit, or an addition to a portfolio you're already building. Conventional guidelines apply, but with a larger down payment and a somewhat higher rate than a primary residence, reflecting the added risk. Some programs qualify you primarily on the property's projected rental income rather than your personal income and debt, which can open the door for investors whose tax returns don't tell the full story. Miami's rental market makes this a common conversation, but I won't promise a return — that depends on the property, not the loan.

required.title: What do you need for an investment property loan?
required.body: Expect a larger down payment than you'd put on a primary residence, along with a credit profile that supports the higher risk lenders take on. Cash reserves after closing are usually required — enough to cover several months of payments. If we go the route of a program that qualifies you on rental income, I'll need a market rent estimate for the property, which an appraiser typically provides. I'll walk through both approaches — income-based and property-based — and show you which one gets you a better result before we commit to either.

how.title: How an investment property loan works
items: Down payments typically higher than for a primary residence.
Rates generally run somewhat above what a primary residence would qualify for.
Some programs qualify you using the property's rental income instead of your own.
Cash reserves after closing are usually required, covering several months of payments.

cashOutRefinance.title: Cash-Out Refinance
cashOutRefinance.description: Turn your home's equity into cash with a cash-out refinance.
cashOutRefinance.heading: Cash-Out Refinance
cashOutRefinance.heroTitle: Turn your home's equity into cash you can use
cashOutRefinance.heroSub: Replace your current mortgage with a larger one and take the difference in cash — for renovations, debt, or your next move.
cashOutRefinance.blurb: Refinance for more than you owe and walk away with the difference — your equity working for you.
cashOutRefinance.intro: A cash-out refinance replaces your current mortgage with a new, larger one, and you keep the difference in cash at closing. People use it to renovate, pay off higher-interest debt, invest, or just build a cushion. It only works if you have enough equity built up, and it comes with real trade-offs I won't gloss over — I'll show you the honest numbers before you decide.

whatIs.title: What is a cash-out refinance?
whatIs.body: A cash-out refinance pays off your existing mortgage with a new loan for a larger amount, and the difference is delivered to you as cash at closing. It's a way to convert equity — the value you've built up in your home — into money you can actually use, without selling the property. Every program requires you to keep a portion of your home's value as equity after the cash-out, so how much you can access depends on your current balance and the home's value, not just what you'd like to take. It's one loan, one payment, not a second lien on top of your first.

required.title: What do you need for a cash-out refinance?
required.body: You need enough equity to both cash out and still leave the required amount behind — I'll calculate that with you using your current balance and an updated home value. Income and credit have to support the new, larger loan amount, same as any refinance. Be honest about the trade-offs going in: your balance goes up, your monthly payment can go up, closing costs apply, and the loan term resets from day one. If the numbers don't clearly work in your favor for what you're trying to do, I'll tell you before we start the paperwork. If you marked cash-out as what you're after in my questionnaire, this is exactly where we pick that up.

how.title: How a cash-out refinance works
items: Replaces your current mortgage with a new, larger loan.
You receive the difference between the two loan amounts as cash at closing.
Requires enough equity to leave a required portion of your home's value untouched.
Your balance, payment, and loan term all reset — I'll show you the real numbers first.

vaRefinance.title: VA Refinance
vaRefinance.description: IRRRL and VA cash-out refinance options for veterans and service members.
vaRefinance.heading: VA Refinance
vaRefinance.heroTitle: Your service keeps opening doors — also when you refinance
vaRefinance.heroSub: Two VA paths: the streamlined IRRRL to lower your rate with minimal paperwork, or a VA cash-out to tap your equity.
vaRefinance.blurb: Rate-lowering streamline (IRRRL) or VA cash-out — refinancing built on your VA benefit.
vaRefinance.intro: VA refinancing comes in two forms, and they solve different problems. The IRRRL is a streamlined VA-to-VA refinance built to lower your rate or payment, or move you off an adjustable rate, with less paperwork than a typical refinance. A VA cash-out refinance goes further — it can tap your home's equity, and it's also how you move a non-VA loan into the VA program. I'll confirm which one, if either, actually helps you before we go further.

whatIs.title: What is a VA refinance?
whatIs.body: A VA refinance uses your VA loan benefit to replace an existing mortgage. The IRRRL — Interest Rate Reduction Refinance Loan — only works if you already have a VA loan, and it's designed to be simple: reduced documentation, no appraisal in most cases, and a straightforward goal of a lower rate, a lower payment, or a switch from an adjustable rate to a fixed one. A VA cash-out refinance is different: it lets you borrow against your home's equity, and unlike the IRRRL, it can also convert a conventional or FHA loan into a VA loan for veterans who qualify. Eligibility for either follows your VA benefit.

required.title: What do you need for a VA refinance?
required.body: For an IRRRL, you need an existing VA loan in good standing and a clear net benefit — a lower rate, payment, or a move to fixed — since VA rules require the refinance to actually help you. A VA cash-out refinance has more in common with a standard refinance: enough equity, income and credit that support the new loan, and a Certificate of Eligibility tied to your service, active duty, or, for some, your spouse's. A funding fee applies in most cases, with exemptions for some borrowers with a service-connected disability, which I'll check for you upfront.

how.title: How a VA refinance works
items: IRRRL: a streamlined VA-to-VA refinance to lower your rate or payment, with reduced paperwork.
VA cash-out: borrow against your equity, or convert a non-VA loan into the VA program.
Eligibility follows your VA benefit — veterans, active duty, and some surviving spouses.
A funding fee applies in most cases, waived for some borrowers with a service-connected disability.

prequalify.title: Pre-Qualify
prequalify.description: Find out what you may qualify for before you start house hunting. A pre-qualification makes you a stronger buyer.
prequalify.heading: Pre-Qualify
prequalify.heroTitle: Walk into every showing as a serious buyer.
prequalify.heroSub: Many agents ask for a pre-qualification before the first visit. Get yours sorted in minutes.

why.title: A pre-qualification tells sellers you're for real.
why.body: Before you fall in love with a home, let's estimate what you may be approved for. With that letter in hand, agents and sellers take your offer seriously — and you shop with a clear budget instead of a guess.

credit.title: Know how your credit looks first.
credit.body: Lenders weigh your payment history, income and current debts. Reviewing your credit report before applying lets you fix surprises early — and if your score is lower than you'd like, we can talk about a plan to get it ready.

calculator.title: Mortgage Calculator
calculator.heading: Mortgage Calculator
calculator.heroTitle: What a payment could actually look like.
calculator.heroSub: The interactive calculator is coming online shortly, alongside the questionnaire. Here's the math it'll run, with a real example.

explain.title: What this estimates
explain.body: A mortgage payment estimate covers principal and interest — what you borrow, plus what it costs to borrow it, spread over the loan term. It won't include property taxes, homeowners insurance, or HOA dues, which vary by property and change your total payment. I always show you the full number, not just the part that looks smaller.

learn.title: Learn
learn.description: Straight answers to the questions I hear most, before you commit to anything.
learn.heading: Learn
learn.heroSub: No sales pitch, no fine print you need a lawyer for — just the questions buyers actually ask me, answered the way I'd answer them on the phone.

items.q: How does buying a home actually work, start to finish?
items.a: Buying a home follows a predictable order, even when it doesn't feel that way. It starts with your numbers — what you can comfortably spend — then pre-qualification, so you know what you can actually offer before you fall for a listing. From there it's the search, an offer, underwriting, where your file gets verified, and closing, when you get the keys. I like to come in at the very first step, not the last one — knowing your budget before you start touring homes saves you from chasing houses you were never going to get.

items.q: What's the difference between pre-qualified and pre-approved?
items.a: Pre-qualification is a fast, honest estimate — you tell me your income, savings, and goals, usually through my questionnaire, and I give you a realistic range without pulling documents. Pre-approval goes further: I verify your income, assets, and credit with actual paperwork, and the result carries real weight when you make an offer, because sellers know it's backed by documentation, not just your word. Start with pre-qualification to get oriented, then move to pre-approval once you're seriously touring homes and ready to compete for one.

items.q: What does a lender look at in my credit?
items.a: I look at your credit as a range, not a wall — it tells me which programs fit you best, not whether you're allowed to buy a home. What matters most is your payment history and how much debt you're actively carrying relative to your income. Different loan programs have different minimums, so a score that rules out one option often still works for another. And nothing here involves a credit pull — when we talk, it's your own honest estimate, so we can talk freely before anything touches your report.

items.q: How much down payment do I really need?
items.a: The idea that you need a huge down payment to buy is one of the most common things keeping good buyers renting longer than they should. Conventional loans start as low as 3% down, FHA as low as 3.5%, and VA or USDA can get qualified buyers all the way to 0% — which program fits you depends on your credit, your income, and the property itself, so that's a conversation, not a guess. And your down payment isn't the only cash you'll need at closing; there are also closing costs to plan for, so I always walk you through the full picture before you commit to a number.

items.q: Can I buy with an ITIN or as a foreign national?
items.a: Yes — this comes up constantly, and it's one of my specialties. Buying with an ITIN instead of a Social Security number, or as a foreign national without U.S. residency, isn't a dead end; there are programs built specifically for these situations. The conditions are different — usually more documentation and a different down payment structure than a standard loan — but the path is real. My questionnaire asks about your status early for exactly this reason: it lets me match you with the right program from the first conversation instead of after you've already fallen for a house.

Refinancing makes sense when it actually moves you forward — a lower rate, a lower monthly payment, dropping mortgage insurance you no longer need, or pulling cash out for a real goal. It doesn't make sense just because rates dropped a little or a lender calls you out of the blue. The number I care about is your break-even point: how long it takes the monthly savings to cover the closing costs of the new loan. If you're planning to stay in the home past that point, it's usually worth it. If not, I'll tell you honestly to wait.

Closing costs are the fees beyond your down payment that make the loan and the sale official — things like the appraisal, title work, loan origination, and prepaid items like taxes and insurance set up in escrow. As a rough order of magnitude, plan for a modest percentage of the purchase price, though the exact number depends on your loan, your property, and your county. You won't have to guess: once you're under contract, you get a Loan Estimate that itemizes every cost in writing, so nothing shows up as a surprise at the closing table.

about.title: About David Herrera
about.description: Licensed Mortgage Loan Originator in Miami, FL.
about.heading: About me
about.heroSub: Mortgage loan originator in Miami. No call center, no hand-offs — the person who answers your first question is the same one at your closing table.
about.mission: My mission is to get you a mortgage you actually understand, from someone who answers the phone.

story.title: How I work
story.body: I work with you in English or Spanish, whichever is more comfortable, and I stay on your file from the first call to the day you get your keys. Most of the people I work with are buying their first home, or their first home in the United States, so I explain each step before I ask you to sign anything.

values.title: What matters to me
items: Clarity — you'll know what you qualify for and what it costs before you commit to anything.
Availability — call, text, or WhatsApp, and I reply the same day.
No pressure — you set the pace, not a sales quota.
Bilingual by default — English or Spanish, whichever you need.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.description: How we handle your personal information.
privacy.heading: Privacy Policy

sections.title: What information we collect
sections.body: When you reach out — through the contact page, WhatsApp, a phone call, or (once it's live) the loan questionnaire — I collect what you give me: your name, phone number, email, and anything you share about your income, credit, or the property you're looking at. I don't collect anything else about you behind the scenes.

sections.title: How we use it
sections.body: Your information is used to answer your questions, prepare a loan quote, and follow up with you about your mortgage. It isn't used for anything beyond that — no unrelated marketing, no resale.

sections.title: Who we share it with
sections.body: Your information stays between you and me, except where it's genuinely needed to move your loan forward — for example, with a lender during the application process. Any customer relationship or email tools we add in a later phase will be documented here before they're used.

sections.title: Your rights
sections.body: You can ask what information I have on file for you, ask me to correct it, or ask me to delete it. Contact me directly and I'll take care of it personally.

sections.title: Cookies
sections.body: This site doesn't use analytics or tracking cookies today. If that changes, this page will say so before it happens.

accessibility.title: Accessibility Statement
accessibility.description: Our commitment to an accessible website.
accessibility.heading: Accessibility Statement

sections.title: Our commitment
sections.body: This site is built to meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA, the standard most commonly used to judge whether a website works for people with disabilities. It's a goal I take seriously, not a checkbox — a mortgage is confusing enough without an inaccessible website in the way.

sections.title: What we've built in
sections.body: Color combinations are checked for contrast, every interactive element works from a keyboard alone, focus is always visible so you can see where you are, and the page structure uses proper HTML headings and landmarks so screen readers can make sense of it.

sections.title: Found a barrier?
sections.body: If any part of this site is hard to use with a screen reader, keyboard, or other assistive technology, tell me directly — the phone, email, and WhatsApp on the contact page all reach me personally — and I'll fix it or find another way to get you the same information.

sections.title: An ongoing effort
sections.body: Accessibility isn't a one-time fix. As this site grows, I'll keep testing it and correcting what falls short.
